study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: The paper presents Neurofind, a new freely available tool that bridges the gap in accessibility for normative modeling in neuroimaging research. It wraps previously tested methods for data harmonization and advanced normative models into a user-friendly, web-based platform requiring minimal user input, aiming to make these techniques available to a broader research community.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Group comparisons of deviation metrics (OIS and BAG) between patients and controls were performed using independent-sample t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests. Associations between deviation metrics and symptom severity were tested using Pearson's or Spearman's correlation. Heterogeneity was assessed using mean pairwise cosine similarity of ROI-level deviation scores.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: A majority of Alzheimer's disease patients (55.2%) showed extreme brain morphology deviations, whereas fewer schizophrenia patients (30.1%) were extreme outliers; both patient groups exhibited signs of accelerated brain aging.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: In Alzheimer's disease, 55.2% of patients showed very extreme Outlier Index Scores, primarily driven by deviations in temporal-limbic structures and ventricles, and these patients showed homogeneous deviation patterns. In contrast, only 30.1% of schizophrenia patients were classified as extreme outliers, with deviations concentrated in the hippocampus and pallidum, and their deviation patterns were more heterogeneous than controls. Both clinical groups displayed evidence of accelerated brain aging.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: The tool is not customizable for advanced users; it is a research tool not intended for clinical diagnosis or prediction; the brain age model does not correct for age-related bias ('regression to the mean'); the harmonization method (Neuroharmony) may not be effective for images with unusual quality metrics; the model's suitability is limited to populations similar to the training set (e.g., age 20-80, specific ethnicities, 1.5T/3T MRI).
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: The development of a practical tool for the wider research community, such as Neuro /uniFB01 nd, comes with a number of limitations and assumptions. Neuro /uniFB01 nd was designed to make normative modelling accessible and therefore it is not customisable...it was not developed to identify speci /uniFB01 c disorders or predict clinical outcomes in a real-world clinical setting. To maintain simplicity and interpretability of the /uniFB01 ndings, the brain age model in Neuro /uniFB01 nd did not take its statistical dependency on chronological age into account...Neuroharmony may not be able to predict the required adjustments if the quality metrics are unusual...Neuro /uniFB01 nd may not be suitable for analysis of subjects that are very different from our training range, i.e., outside of ages 20 -80, non-white ethnicities, or MRI scans acquired with /uniFB01 elds of strength considerably lower or higher than 1.5 T or 3 T. Finally, it is important to note that Neuro /uniFB01 nd is a research tool, so results should not be used to make clinical decisions.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study's primary output is a practical, freely available, web-based tool called 'Neurofind' (www.neurofind.ai), designed to make normative modeling accessible to non-expert researchers. The paper includes a step-by-step guide for using the tool.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This paper introduces 'Neurofind', a novel, freely accessible web-based tool (www.neurofind.ai) designed to perform normative modeling on structural MRI data. A key contribution is the tool itself, which implements data harmonization, an Adversarial Autoencoder for outlier detection, and a Support Vector Regression model for brain age prediction. The paper serves as a manual and validation study for this tool, providing exemplar applications in Alzheimer's disease and schizophrenia to demonstrate its utility and interpretability.
